## Ezra 9 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview

The chapter divides naturally: vv. 1–2 (the report of intermarriage brought to Ezra), vv. 3–4 (Ezra's horrified response), and vv. 5–15 (Ezra's prayer of confession). All consulted sources agree this is one of the great penitential prayers of Scripture, alongside Nehemiah 9 and Daniel 9.

---

### v. 1 — "After these things had been accomplished, the leaders approached me…"

**Traditional Reading:**

The "things accomplished" refer to the delivery of the king's commissions, the weighing of the temple vessels, and the sacrifices just offered (Ezra 8:33–36). The "leaders" (princes) who approached Ezra were civil heads of the community whom Ezra found governing on his arrival; his own authority did not wholly supersede theirs (Pulpit). Gill notes these were the most religious among the nobles, concerned about corruption but too few in number to reform it themselves. Ellicott observes it is remarkable that complaint on a matter of religious transgression came from secular rather than ecclesiastical authorities — but the priestly families were themselves implicated in the sin (Ezra 10:18).

The sin reported was that the people, priests, and Levites had "not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands, with respect to their abominations." The problem was primarily religious, not ethnic — they failed to separate from the idolatrous practices ("abominations") of these nations. Guzik (Enduring Word) writes: "The root problem wasn't ethnic but spiritual: the people weren't separating from the abominations (idolatry) of surrounding nations."

The list of nations echoes the pre-conquest inhabitants of Canaan (Exodus 34:11–16; Deuteronomy 7:1–4). Pulpit notes that by Ezra's time only the Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites were still extant as identifiable peoples; the older names were used to make the case as hateful as possible (Ellicott).

### v. 2 — "the holy seed has been mixed with the people of the land… leaders and officials have taken the lead in this unfaithfulness"

**Traditional Reading:**

The "holy seed" — a term from Isaiah 6:13 — refers to Israel as a people set apart by divine call (Exodus 19:6). Pulpit explains: however much Israel polluted itself, it was still "holy" by profession, call, and obligation. By intermarrying, they frustrated God's whole purpose in separating a "peculiar people." Guzik notes that if intermarriage with idolaters continued, "in a few generations there would cease to be any distinctive Jewish community in the Promised Land."

The leaders were "foremost" (literally "first") in this trespass. Gill says they were "ringleaders" who should by authority and example have restrained others. Constable notes the Mosaic Law strictly forbade intermarriage with native Canaanites (Exodus 34:11–16; Deuteronomy 7:1–5), and earlier history showed its tragic consequences (1 Kings 11:1–8).

**Denominational / Cross-Tradition Perspectives:**

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Stresses that the problem was *not* racial. Scripture never forbids intermarriage merely because of different racial or cultural backgrounds. Moses married Zipporah the Midianite without divine displeasure; Ruth the Moabitess was incorporated into the royal line after conversion. The sin was marrying *impenitent pagans* — people who would bring their false worship into Israelite homes. The issue was remaining free from "abominations — the false moral and religious beliefs and practices of pagan peoples." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/problem-of-intermarriage

- **Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper):** Same emphasis: "the reason for this prohibition is not racial, but religious." All the relevant texts are religiously grounded, not racially grounded. The only New Testament marriage constraint on a believer is to marry a believer (1 Corinthians 7:39; 2 Corinthians 6:14). Piper notes there are approved "inter-people" marriages in the Bible (e.g., Rahab, Ruth, Zipporah). — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-ethics-of-interracial-marriage-session-5

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** Guzik writes, "This shows that the problem was not primarily ethnic. The problem was they did not separate themselves from these abominations, specifically the idolatry of these people." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-9/

**Modern Scholarship:**

Bible Odyssey notes that the intermarriage narrative in Ezra-Nehemiah "betrays increased awareness of ethnic identity among those returning from exile." It describes two groups: those returning from exile who called themselves the "Holy Seed" and wished to remain pure, and those who remained on the land. The text "actively constructs negative ideas about deep ethnic difference between the groups and then makes the differences matter." This reflects a postexilic social dynamic where maintaining community identity while in a foreign culture became a pressing concern. — https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/intermarriage-in-ezra-nehemiah/

### v. 3 — "I tore my tunic and cloak, pulled out some hair from my head and beard, and sat down in horror"

**Traditional Reading:**

Ezra's actions express extreme horror and grief. Rending clothes was a standard Oriental sign of grief (Genesis 37:29, 34; Job 1:20; 2 Samuel 1:2). Plucking hair from head and beard was more unusual — Pulpit notes this practice is not elsewhere attested in canonical Scripture (only in the Apocrypha: 1 Esdras 8:71; 2 Esdras 1:8). Gill explains he did not shave (which would transgress Leviticus 19:27) but plucked the hair out, showing extreme sorrow.

The word "astonied" (KJV) or "horror" (BSB) translates a Hebrew verb meaning "to be appalled, stupefied." Yamauchi (cited by Guzik) notes the English word originally meant "to make pale." Guzik comments: "Rare is the soul who is so shocked at disobedience that he is appalled." Ezra knew that these same sins of idolatry and compromise had caused the exile in the first place.

Guzik adds a vivid comparison: "Both Ezra and Nehemiah were confronted with the sin of pagan intermarriage. Nehemiah responded by plucking out the hair of the guilty (Nehemiah 13:25); Ezra responded by plucking out his own hair."

### v. 4 — "everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel gathered around me… until the evening offering"

**Traditional Reading:**

"Everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel" refers not merely to all God-fearing persons (cf. Isaiah 66:2) but specifically those alarmed at the transgression of God's commands and at the threats the Law contained against transgressors (Deuteronomy 7:4) — Pulpit. Gill says they had "a reverence for the word of God" and "feared to break the laws of God, and trembled at his judgments."

The phrase "transgression of those that had been carried away" is significant. Ellicott notes this was the usual name for the returned exiles ("the children of the captivity," Ezra 4:1). They had *not* been guilty of this sin during the exile itself; it was an aggravation that they committed it *after* their gracious return.

Ezra sat astonished from morning (when the report was made) until the evening sacrifice at about 3 p.m. — "speechless and motionless — for several hours" (Pulpit). Guzik says: "He no doubt wondered how the people could endanger themselves like this again."

**Denominational note — Pentecostal/Charismatic:**

Guzik (Enduring Word) says these who trembled "were marked by their respect for God's word" and adds a spiritual insight: "In a real spiritual sense, they were carried away captive by their sin of partnership with idolaters and idolatry."

### v. 5 — "At the evening offering, I got up from my humiliation… fell on my knees, spread out my hands to the LORD my God"

**Traditional Reading:**

The "evening sacrifice" (about 3 p.m.) was the appointed time for prayer and confession (cf. Acts 3:1). Pulpit says: "The time of sacrifice was the fittest time for prayer, especially for a prayer in which acknowledgment of sin was to form a large part. Sacrifice symbolized expiation." Gill notes that Ezra had been fasting all day ("from my fasting" / "from my heaviness").

Ezra tore his garments a *second* time — a renewed indication of sorrow meant to impress the gathered crowd and stir them to penitence (Pulpit).

His posture — kneeling with hands spread out — was typical of Jewish prayer. Guzik surveys the many biblical examples of kneeling prayer (Solomon, Daniel, Stephen, Peter, Paul, Jesus) and notes: "The Bible has enough prayer not on the knees to show us that it isn't required, but it also has enough prayer on the knees to show us that it is good." Spread hands toward heaven signified surrender, openness, and ready reception.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-9.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-9.html

### v. 6 — "O my God, I am ashamed and embarrassed to lift up my face to You… our iniquities are higher than our heads, and our guilt has reached the heavens"

**Traditional Reading:**

The prayer begins with "O my God" — a confession of personal covenant faith — but Ezra speaks representatively for the whole nation. Pulpit calls this "the most remarkable feature of Ezra's confession": the thoroughness with which he identifies himself with erring countrymen. "All their sins he appears to consider as his sins."

Ezra begins with shame (two Hebrew words: one for being ashamed, one for the pain accompanying shame — Yamauchi, cited by Guzik). Jeremiah had complained that in his day people "were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush" (Jeremiah 6:15; 8:12). Ezra begins by protesting that he *does* blush and burn with shame (Pulpit).

"Our iniquities are increased over our head" — like a flood overwhelming them (Psalm 38:4). "Our trespass is grown up unto the heavens" — so great that it has attracted God's notice and anger (Pulpit). Gill adds the image of sins "piled up in heaps, reaching to heaven, and calling down vengeance from thence."

Guzik stresses that Ezra said "**our** iniquities," not "their iniquities." Ezra had just arrived and had not participated in this sin, but "because they were bound together in the same covenant before God, their iniquities were in fact his."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-9.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-9.html

### v. 7 — "From the days of our fathers to this day, our guilt has been great… delivered into the hands of the kings of the earth… as we are this day"

**Traditional Reading:**

Ezra traces a continuous history of national guilt. Ellicott notes that in the "Common Prayers" of Ezra, Nehemiah, and Daniel, "the race of Israel is regarded as one, and national sins as one 'great trespass.'" The repetition of "this day" at beginning and end of the verse is emphatic: first in reference to ongoing sin, then in reference to ongoing punishment.

Pulpit lists the specific kings into whose hands Israel was delivered: Menahem to Pul, Pekah to Tiglath-Pileser, Hoshea to Shalmaneser/Sargon, Manasseh to Esarhaddon, and the line of Judean kings (Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, Zedekiah) to Nebuchadnezzar. The priests shared fully in these calamities (2 Kings 25:18; Ezekiel 1:1–3).

"Confusion of face" (KJV) means disgrace and open shame (Psalm 44:13–15). Precept Austin notes that Ezra's prayer "reveals where the nation's sins had led them: 'on account of our iniquities we, our kings and our priests have been given into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, and to plunder and to open shame.'"

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-9.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-9.html

### v. 8 — "But now, for a brief moment, grace has come from the LORD… a remnant… a stake in His holy place… new life and light to our eyes"

**Traditional Reading:**

"A little space" (KJV) or "brief moment" — Ellicott says the "little" is emphatic. The period from Cyrus's decree to Ezra's time was nearly two generations, but "it was a moment only in relation to the past and the possible future." The idea inverts Isaiah 54:7: "For a small moment have I forsaken thee."

"A nail in his holy place" (KJV) or "a stake in His holy place" — Gill says this means "a fixed settlement in the land of Judea… a prince of their own, Zerubbabel, to be the governor of them" (cf. Isaiah 22:23). Ellicott interprets it differently: "The Temple was itself the sure nail on which all their hopes hung." Guzik explains that in ancient houses, things were stored on pegs set around the room; if something was on its peg, it was safe and secure, stored properly and ready for use. Only days before this prayer, Ezra had seen the temple for the first time.

"A little reviving" or "new life" — literally "make us a little life" (Ellicott). The current revival was but the beginning and still precarious. Guzik: "Ezra rejoiced to see even a measure of revival and knew that this was an emblem of God's mercy and favor that should not be despised."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-9.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-9.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-9/

### v. 9 — "Though we are slaves, our God has not forsaken us… grace in the sight of the kings of Persia… a wall of protection"

**Traditional Reading:**

"We were bondmen" (KJV) or "we are slaves" — Ellicott says "better, we are bondmen. In this lies the emphasis of the appeal." The Jews had not recovered political independence; they remained subjects of the Persian crown. Yet God extended mercy "in the sight of the kings of Persia" — moving Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes to favor them.

"A wall in Judah and Jerusalem" — this is figurative, as the literal city wall was not yet rebuilt (that awaited Nehemiah). Gill says the "wall" refers to "the protection of the kings of Persia, which was a fence to them against the Samaritans and others; and especially the hedge of divine Providence about them." Ellicott similarly says it is "a figurative expression for security." Guzik cites Trapp: "They had the fence of the king of Persia's favour. They had also God's providence, as a hedge or wall of fire round about them."

Some critics take this reference to a wall as evidence for the priority of Nehemiah over Ezra, assuming a literal wall had been rebuilt, but "most scholars agree that the reference here is not to be taken literally" (Yamauchi, cited by Guzik).

**Note on tradition:** No significant denominational differences were found on this verse.

### v. 10 — "And now, our God, what can we say after this? For we have forsaken the commandments"

**Traditional Reading:**

The shift from "my God" (v. 6) to "our God" (v. 10) is deliberate: Ezra has fully taken on the representative role. Ellicott notes the prayer never returns to the first person singular from this point.

"What shall we say after this?" — after all God's mercy just recounted. There is no excuse, no defence. Gill: "What apology or excuse can be made for such ingratitude? what can be said in favour of such a people?" Guzik: "Ezra offered no excuses and not even an explanation. Their conduct was indefensible and in direct disobedience to what God commanded."

Pulpit captures the pathos: "But all was a mercy for which there had been no adequate return."

### vv. 11–12 — "The land that you are entering… is a land polluted… do not give your daughters… never seek their peace or prosperity"

**Traditional Reading:**

Ezra does not quote a single passage verbatim; he summarizes the substance of multiple prophetic commands. Ellicott: "In the later Old Testament Scriptures the quotation of the earlier is often of this character, giving the substance of many passages." The key sources are Deuteronomy 7:3 (the only place where the interdict includes both daughters and sons) and Deuteronomy 23:6 ("nor seek their peace").

The land is called "unclean" — this refers not merely to idolatry but to the incestuous marriages and impure practices of the Canaanites, on account of which God "spewed out the old inhabitants" (Gill, referencing Leviticus 18).

"Never seek their peace or prosperity" — an echo of the stern injunction regarding Moabites and Ammonites (Deuteronomy 23:6). Ellicott observes: "It is observable that the giving of daughters in marriage to heathens is not mentioned either in Ezra or in Nehemiah" — apparently it was not happening.

"That you may be strong and eat the good of the land" — Guzik cites Poole: "Although you may fancy that this way of making leagues and marriages with them is the only way to establish and settle you, yet I assure you it will weaken and ruin you and the contrary course will make you stronger."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-9.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-9.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-9/

### v. 13 — "After all that has come upon us… You, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserve"

**Traditional Reading:**

This is one of the most remarkable theological acknowledgments in Scripture. After the horrors of exile — the sword, captivity, pillage, and humiliation — Ezra says God punished them *less* than they deserved. Gill (citing Jarchi): "Thou hast refrained thyself from exacting of us all our sins, and hast exacted of us beneath our sins (or less than they deserve), and hast not taken vengeance on us according to all our sins." The deserved punishment was eternal; what they received was temporal and moderated.

Pulpit: "If neither severity nor kindness avail anything, what can God do more? must he not view our case as hopeless, and so make an end of us altogether? (Compare Isaiah 5:1–7; Luke 13:6–9)."

Guzik: "As severe as the exile was, Ezra recognized that it was less than the people of God deserved." Precept Austin adds that this is one of four elements of genuine confession: "Confession acknowledges the absolute righteousness of God in all His dealings with us."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-9.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-9.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-9/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-9-commentary

### v. 14 — "shall we again break Your commandments… Would You not become so angry with us as to wipe us out, leaving no remnant or survivor?"

**Traditional Reading:**

This is a rhetorical question whose answer is self-evident: yes, God would be just to consume them entirely. Pulpit: "If after their deliverance they again fell away, the sin could not but be unpardonable; and the punishment to be expected was a final uprooting and destruction from which there could be no recovery."

Ellicott notes that all the tokens of mercy listed in vv. 8–9 are "conditional in their continuance." Continued sin in the face of recent mercy would exhaust God's patience.

Precept Austin notes the repeated emphasis on "remnant" — four times in this prayer (vv. 8, 13, 14, 15) — "showing how the formerly strong nation had been decimated." If they do not repent, God may destroy them "so that no remnant survives or escapes."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-9.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-9.html
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-9-commentary

### v. 15 — "O LORD, God of Israel, You are righteous! … Here we are before You in our guilt, though because of it no one can stand before You."

**Traditional Reading:**

This is the climax and summary of the whole prayer. "You are righteous" — tsaddiq — Ellicott says this "solemn invocation shows that this is a summary of the whole prayer: God's righteousness is magnified, as accompanied by the grace which had preserved them." Pulpit offers an alternative: "Righteousness, in its widest sense, includes mercy; and so the meaning here may be, 'Thou art good and gracious; of which thy having spared us is a proof.'"

Guzik highlights three wise elements in Ezra's appeal: (1) he appeals to the LORD as "God of Israel" — though Israel had been unfaithful, Ezra still hoped for covenant mercies; (2) he appeals to God's righteousness in preserving a remnant in fulfillment of prior promises (Isaiah 10:20–22); (3) he makes no excuses — "Ezra wisely did not claim an excuse or a reason for their sin."

Gill: "We cannot defend ourselves; we cannot plead ignorance of the divine commands; we have nothing to say for ourselves why judgment should not be passed upon us; we leave ourselves in thine hands, and at thy mercy."

Guzik cites Kidner: "Ezra had not even the heart to plead, as Moses had, that God's name would suffer in such a case. His prayer was naked confession, without excuses, without the pressure of so much as a request."

Precept Austin observes that Ezra's prayer "makes no petition, but rather, he implicitly casts himself and the nation on God's undeserved mercy." The prayer was made at the time of the evening offering — "Perhaps the smell of the sacrifice encouraged his heart that God has made a way for sinners to be reconciled to Him, namely, through the shedding of the blood of a substitute."

**Reformed perspective (Ligonier):** "The prayer also admits that the sin of intermarriage proves that the Jews did not learn the lesson of the exile and return. A more dramatic act of God's saving power would be needed to bring in the full restoration blessings for the Lord's people (Luke 2:22–38)." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/problem-of-intermarriage

### Summary of Tradition-Specific Readings

| Topic | Shared View | Distinctive Emphasis |
|---|---|---|
| **Nature of the sin** | All agree it was the intermarriage with idolatrous pagans | Reformed (Ligonier) and Baptist (Piper/Desiring God) strongly emphasise it was religious, not racial — linking to the NT principle of marrying "only in the Lord." Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey) focuses on ethnic identity construction in the postexilic community |
| **Ezra's prayer as model** | All traditions treat it as a model of penitential confession | Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik) emphasises the felt grief, the hours of "astonishment," and the spontaneity of the Spirit-led response. Reformed (Ligonier) links it to the Westminster Shorter Catechism definition of repentance (WSC 87) |
| **"Holy seed" (v. 2)** | All agree it refers to Israel's set-apart status by covenant | Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey) sees it as a self-designation of the returning exile group to distinguish themselves from "the people of the land" who had not been through the exile |
| **The "wall" (v. 9)** | All agree it is figurative, not the literal city wall | Debate exists only among critical scholars about chronological implications for the Ezra-Nehemiah relationship (noted by Yamauchi/Guizik); all traditional commentators treat it as metaphorical for divine protection |
